title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 167 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 803–805 (Night 167, continuing directly from nights-166), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 167 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The slave-girl brings the jeweller the money, and he uses it to repay what he owed and to have his stripped house rebuilt. Then he goes to ʿAlī, who has been asking for him night and day and lies between faint and stupor; at the jeweller's visit he revives, eats, and gives him rich furnishings in place of those he lost. In the morning ʿAlī tells him that love ends in death or union, that he is like a bird in a cage, and speaks two lines of verse. Back at his house the jeweller finds the slave-girl in tears: a maid who fled a beating has told the doorkeeper everything, word has reached the Caliph, and Shams al-Nahār has been taken into the palace under a guard of twenty eunuchs. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-seventh night,
sentences.n: The heading is built as before: al-sābiʿa, “the seventh”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَوْهَرِىَّ لَمَّا قَالَتْ لَهُ الْجَارِيَةُ قِفْ هُنَا حَتَّى أَعُودَ إِلَيْكَ وَمَضَتْ ثُمَّ عَادَتْ وَهِيَ حَامِلَةٌ الْمَالَ وَرَفَعَتْهُ إِلَيَّ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jawhariyya lammā qālat lahu al-jāriyatu qif hunā ḥattā aʿūda ilayka wa-maḍat thumma ʿādat wa-hiya ḥāmilatun al-māla wa-rafaʿathu ilayya
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller, when the slave-girl said to-him: Stand here until I-return to-you, and she-went-off; then she-came-back, and she (was) carrying the money, and she-raised-it to-me.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said: When the slave-girl had told me, “Wait here until I come back to you,” she went off; then she came back carrying the money, and handed it over to me.
sentences.n: The night opens by repeating the last words of the one before. The sentence sets out in the third person, “that the jeweller, when the slave-girl said to him …”, and then, without finishing that frame, slips into the jeweller's own voice: rafaʿathu ilayya, “she handed it up to me”. The tale is his, and from here on he tells it; the idiomatic layer supplies the “said” the Arabic leaves out. qif, imperative of waqafa, “stand, stop”; ḥattā aʿūda, “until I return”, subjunctive of a time still to come. wa-hiya ḥāmilatun al-māla, “she carrying the money”, a circumstantial clause; the participle takes al-māla as its object as a verb would (in construct, ḥāmilatu al-māli, is equally possible). rafaʿa ilā, “to raise to”, to hand over. الجوهرى is printed with final ى; the shadda of اليّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِي يَا سَيِّدِى نَجْتَمِعُ بِكَ فِي أَيِّ مَحَلٍّ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lī yā sayyidī najtamiʿu bika fī ayyi maḥallin
sentences.l: And she-said to-me: O my-master, we-meet with-you in which place?
sentences.i: And she said to me, “Sir, where are we to meet you?”
sentences.n: ijtamaʿa bi-, “to meet with”: bi- marks the one met. The “we” is the slave-girl speaking for her mistress and herself. The question has no question particle; fī ayyi maḥallin, “in what place”, carries it. سيدى is printed with final ى.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا أَمْضِي وَأَتَوَجَّهُ إِلَى دَارِي فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ وَأَتَحَمَّلُ الصُّعُوبَةَ لِأَجْلِ خَاطِرِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā amḍī wa-atawajjahu ilā dārī fī hādhihi al-sāʿati wa-ataḥammalu al-ṣuʿūbata li-ajli khāṭiriki
sentences.l: And I-said to-her: I-go and I-head to my-house in this hour, and I-bear the difficulty for-the-sake-of your-mind,
sentences.i: I said to her, “I shall go off now and make for my house this very hour, and take the trouble on myself for your sake,
sentences.n: amḍī is read as “I go”, the first of a run of first-person verbs (atawajjahu, ataḥammalu, and atadabbaru in the next sentence), the imperfect looking to what he is about to do. The same letters would also read imḍī, “go!”, said to the girl, sending her off; but the run of “I” verbs favours amḍī. tawajjaha ilā, “to turn one's face to”, make for. taḥammala, Form V, “to take on oneself”. li-ajli khāṭiriki, “for the sake of your mind”: khāṭir, “mind, feelings”, and li-ajli khāṭiri someone is the everyday “to please someone”, for someone's sake.

sentences.t: وَأَتَدَبَّرُ فِيمَا يُوصِلُكِ إِلَيْهِ فَإِنَّهُ يَتَعَذَّرُ الْوُصُولُ إِلَيْهِ فِي هَذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: wa-atadabbaru fīmā yūṣiluki ilayhi fa-innahu yataʿadhdharu al-wuṣūlu ilayhi fī hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: and I-take-thought in what will-bring-you to-him; for it (is that) the reaching to-him is-impossible in this time.
sentences.i: and think out some way of bringing you to him; for there is no getting to him at this hour.”
sentences.n: tadabbara fī, Form V, “to ponder”, here to work out a plan for. mā yūṣiluki ilayhi, “what will bring you to him”: awṣala, Form IV of waṣala, “to make arrive”; “him” is ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, whom the girl was sent to ask after. fa-innahu, “for it is (the case that)”: the -hu points to the whole clause that follows, not to a person. taʿadhdhara, Form V, “to be impossible”, with al-wuṣūl, “getting there”, as its subject.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ فَأَخْبِرْنِي بِمَحَلٍّ آتِيكَ فِيهِ فَقُلْتُ لَهَا فِي دَارِي
sentences.tr: qālat fa-akhbirnī bi-maḥallin ātīka fīhi fa-qultu lahā fī dārī
sentences.l: She-said: Then inform-me of a-place I-come-to-you in-it. And I-said to-her: In my-house.
sentences.i: She said, “Then tell me of a place where I may come to you.” I said to her, “At my house.”
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to inform (someone) of”: bi- marks the thing told. maḥallin ātīka fīhi, “a place I may come to you in”: an indefinite noun takes its relative clause without alladhī, and fīhi takes up the place again. The madda of آتيك is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَدَّعَتْنِي وَمَضَتْ فَحَمَلْتُ الْمَالَ وَأَتَيْتُ بِهِ إِلَى مَنْزِلِي
sentences.tr: thumma waddaʿatnī wa-maḍat fa-ḥamaltu al-māla wa-ataytu bihi ilā manzilī
sentences.l: Then she-bade-farewell-to-me and she-went-off, and I-carried the money and I-came with-it to my-dwelling.
sentences.i: Then she took her leave of me and went, and I carried the money home.
sentences.n: waddaʿa, Form II, “to bid farewell to”; its shadda is printed. atā bi-, “to come with”, to bring. manzil, “place of alighting”, one's house.

sentences.t: وَعَدَدْتُ الْمَالَ فَوَجَدْتُهُ خَمْسَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿadadtu al-māla fa-wajadtuhu khamsata ālāfi dīnārin
sentences.l: And I-counted the money, and I-found-it five thousands (of) dinar.
sentences.i: I counted the money and found it came to five thousand dinars.
sentences.n: ʿadadtu: the doubled verb ʿadda keeps its two dāls apart before a consonant ending, as Classical does. wajada with two objects, “to find (something) to be”. khamsata ālāfi: a numeral from three to ten takes its noun in the genitive plural, and takes the -a ending when the noun (alf) is masculine; after alf, dīnār stands in the singular genitive. The madda of آلاف is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَعْطَيْتُ أَهْلِي مِنْهُ شَيْأً وَمَنْ كَانَ لَهُ عِنْدِي شَيْءٌ أَعْطَيْتُهُ عِوَضًا عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-aʿṭaytu ahlī minhu shayʾan wa-man kāna lahu ʿindī shayʾun aʿṭaytuhu ʿiwaḍan ʿanhu
sentences.l: And I-gave my-family of-it something; and whoever there-was for-him with-me something, I-gave-him a-replacement for-it.
sentences.i: I gave some of it to my family, and to everyone who had had anything of his in my keeping I gave its worth in return.
sentences.n: ahl, “people (of a house)”, family. man kāna lahu ʿindī shayʾun, “whoever had a thing with me”: these are the friends whose goods the jeweller had borrowed and lost. The clause stands at the head as a topic, and the -hu of aʿṭaytuhu, “I gave him”, takes it up. ʿiwaḍan ʿanhu, “as a replacement for it”, an accusative of purpose. شيأ is printed with the hamza on the accusative alif, as before; the hamza of شيء is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي قُمْتُ وَأَخَذْتُ غِلْمَانِي وَذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الدَّارِ الَّتِي ضَاعَتْ مِنْهَا الْأَمْتِعَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma innī qumtu wa-akhadhtu ghilmānī wa-dhahabtu ilā al-dāri allatī ḍāʿat minhā al-amtiʿatu
sentences.l: Then (indeed) I rose, and I-took my-lads, and I-went to the house which the goods were-lost from-it.
sentences.i: Then I set to work: I took my servants and went to the house from which the goods had been lost.
sentences.n: thumma innī, “then I”: inna after thumma marks the next step in the story, as before. qumtu, “I rose”, I set about it. ghilmān, plural of ghulām, “lad”, serving-man. allatī ḍāʿat minhā, “which … were lost from it”: minhā takes up “the house” inside the relative clause. This is the house the lovers were carried off from, which the thieves stripped.

sentences.t: وَجِئْتُ بِالْمِعْمَارِينَ وَالنَّجَّارِينَ وَالْبَنَّائِينَ فَأَعَادُوهَا إِلَى مَا كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-jiʾtu bi-al-miʿmārīna wa-al-najjārīna wa-al-bannāʾīna fa-aʿādūhā ilā mā kānat ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And I-came with the master-builders and the carpenters and the masons, and they-returned-it to what it-was upon-it.
sentences.i: I brought in master-builders, carpenters and masons, and they put it back as it had been.
sentences.n: jāʾa bi-, “to come with”, to bring. miʿmār, “master-builder”, here with a sound plural, miʿmārīn; najjār, “carpenter”; bannāʾ, “builder, mason”. aʿāda ilā mā kānat ʿalayhi, “returned it to what it was upon”, restored it to its former state: ʿalā of the state a thing is in. The shaddas of النجّارين and البنّائين and the hamza of جئت and البنّائين are printed.

sentences.t: وَجَعَلْتُ جَارِيَتِي فِيهَا وَنَسِيتُ مَاجَرَى لِي
sentences.tr: wa-jaʿaltu jāriyatī fīhā wa-nasītu mā jarā lī
sentences.l: And I-put my-slave-girl in-it, and I-forgot what happened to-me.
sentences.i: I put my slave-girl in it, and forgot all that had befallen me.
sentences.n: jaʿala fī, “to put in”, to install there. The print runs mā and jarā together (ماجرى); it is kept as one word. The dammas of جعلتُ and نسيتُ, which mark the “I”, are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَمَشَّيْتُ وَأَتَيْتُ إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: thumma tamashshaytu wa-ataytu ilā dāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: Then I-walked-along, and I-came to the house of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.i: Then I walked over to the house of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.n: tamashshā, Form V of mashā, “to walk, stroll”, go on foot. atā ilā, “to come to”: Classical atā takes its object directly.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلْتُ إِلَيْهَا أَقْبَلَ غِلْمَانُهُ عَلَيَّ وَقَالُوا لِي إِنَّ سَيِّدِي فِي طَلَبِكَ لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا وَوَعَدَنَا أَنَّ كُلَّ مَنْ أَتَى بِكَ إِلَيْهِ يُعْتِقُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣaltu ilayhā aqbala ghilmānuhu ʿalayya wa-qālū lī inna sayyidī fī ṭalabika laylan wa-nahāran wa-waʿadanā anna kulla man atā bika ilayhi yuʿtiquhu
sentences.l: And when I-arrived to-it, his-lads came-forward upon-me, and they-said to-me: Indeed my-master (is) in seeking-you night and day, and he-promised-us that every-one who comes with-you to-him, he-will-free-him.
sentences.i: When I reached it, his servants came up to me and said, “Our master has been seeking you night and day, and has promised us that whoever brings you to him he will set free.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to come toward”, approach. sayyidī, “my master”, each servant speaking for himself. fī ṭalabika, “in pursuit of you”; laylan wa-nahāran, accusatives of time. waʿada with anna, “to promise that”; the fatḥa of ووعدَنا is printed and fixes it as waʿadanā, “he promised us”. kulla man atā bika ilayhi, “every one who brings you to him”, put first as a topic and taken up by the -hu of yuʿtiquhu, “he will free him”: aʿtaqa, Form IV, “to set (a slave) free”, so the servants are his slaves. The shadda of عليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَهُمْ يَدُورُونَ وَيُفَتِّشُونَ عَلَيْكَ وَلَا يَعْرِفُونَ لَكَ مَوْضِعًا
sentences.tr: fa-hum yadūrūna wa-yufattishūna ʿalayka wa-lā yaʿrifūna laka mawḍiʿan
sentences.l: So they (are) going-round and searching for-you, and they-do-not know for-you a-place.
sentences.i: So they are going all about searching for you, and nobody knows where you are to be found.
sentences.n: fa-hum, “so they”: the servants speak of the household's searchers in the third person, or the jeweller has slipped into reporting what they told him; the sense is plain either way. fattasha, Form II, “to search”; with ʿalā, “to search for”, a later usage (Classical fattasha takes what is searched through directly). The shadda of يفتّشون is printed. lā yaʿrifūna laka mawḍiʿan, “they know no place for you”, your whereabouts.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ رَجَعَتْ إِلَى سَيِّدِنَا عَافِيَتُهُ فَهُوَ تَارَةً يُفِيقُ وَتَارَةً يَسْتَغْرِقُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad rajaʿat ilā sayyidinā ʿāfiyatuhu fa-huwa tāratan yufīqu wa-tāratan yastaghriqu
sentences.l: And (already) there-has-returned to our-master his-health; so he (is) one-time coming-round and one-time sinking-deep.
sentences.i: Our master's health has begun to come back to him: at times he comes to himself, and at times he sinks away again.
sentences.n: ʿāfiyatuhu, “his well-being”, is the subject, placed after the verb and its ilā-phrase; the sukūn of رجعتْ, printed, shows the feminine verb agreeing with it. tāratan … tāratan, “one time … another time”, now … now. afāqa, Form IV, “to come to oneself”; istaghraqa, Form X, “to be sunk deep”, in a stupor.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا يُفِيقُ يَذْكُرُكَ وَيَقُولُ لَابُدَّ أَنْ تُحْضِرُوهُ لِي لَحْظَةً وَيَعُودُ إِلَى سَكْرَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā yufīqu yadhkuruka wa-yaqūlu lā budda an tuḥḍirūhu lī laḥẓatan wa-yaʿūdu ilā sakratihi
sentences.l: And when he-comes-round he-mentions-you and he-says: No-escape that you-bring-him to-me (for) a-moment; and he-returns to his-stupor.
sentences.i: Whenever he comes round he speaks of you and says, ‘You must bring him to me, if only for a moment’; and then he sinks back into his stupor.”
sentences.n: lammā with the imperfect, “whenever”, of something that keeps happening, a later usage (Classical lammā takes the perfect). lā budda an, “there is no escape from”, you must; the print sets it as one word (لابد). tuḥḍirūhu, “that you (pl.) bring him”, subjunctive after an. laḥẓatan, “a glance's while”, a moment: read here with what goes before, “bring him to me for a moment”; it could also go with what follows, “and after a moment he relapses”. sakra, “drunkenness”, here the stupor of his sickness.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَمَضَيْتُ مَعَ الْغُلَامِ إِلَيْهِ فَوَجَدْتُهُ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُ الْكَلَامَ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-maḍaytu maʿa al-ghulāmi ilayhi fa-wajadtuhu lā yastaṭīʿu al-kalāma
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And I-went with the lad to-him, and I-found-him (he) is-not able the speech.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: So I went with the servant to him, and found him unable to speak.
sentences.n: qāla al-jawharī, “the jeweller said”, reminds the listener whose story this is. wajadtuhu lā yastaṭīʿu, “I found him (that) he could not”: a verb clause stands as the second object of wajada. istaṭāʿa, Form X, “to be able to”, takes its object directly.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهُ جَلَسْتُ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ فَفَتَحَ عَيْنَيْهِ فَلَمَّا رَآنِي بَكَى وَقَالَ لِي أَهْلًا وَمَرْحَبًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhu jalastu ʿinda raʾsihi fa-fataḥa ʿaynayhi fa-lammā raʾānī bakā wa-qāla lī ahlan wa-marḥaban
sentences.l: And when I-saw-him, I-sat by his-head; and he-opened his-two-eyes, and when he-saw-me he-wept, and he-said to-me: Family and welcome!
sentences.i: When I saw him I sat down at his head, and he opened his eyes; and when he saw me he wept and said to me, “Welcome, welcome!”
sentences.n: ahlan wa-marḥaban, accusatives of an unspoken verb, “(you have come to) family and (found) room”, the common greeting of welcome. The hamza of رأيته and رأسه and the madda of رآني are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَسْنَدْتُهُ وَأَجْلَسْتُهُ وَضَمَمْتُهُ إِلَى صَدْرِي
sentences.tr: thumma asnadtuhu wa-ajlastuhu wa-ḍamamtuhu ilā ṣadrī
sentences.l: Then I-propped-him, and I-made-him-sit, and I-pressed-him to my-chest.
sentences.i: Then I propped him up, sat him upright, and held him to my breast.
sentences.n: asnada, Form IV, “to make lean, prop up”; ajlasa, Form IV of jalasa, “to make sit”. ḍamma ilā, “to press to”; ḍamamtu keeps its doubled letter apart before the ending, as Classical does.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِي اعْلَمْ يَا أَخِي أَنِّي مِنْ حِينِ رَقَدْتُ مَا جَلَسْتُ إِلَّا فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ فَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى مُشَاهَدَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lī iʿlam yā akhī annī min ḥīni raqadtu mā jalastu illā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati fa-al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi ʿalā mushāhadatika
sentences.l: And he-said to-me: Know, O my-brother, that-I, from (the) time I-lay-down, did-not sit except in this hour; so the praise (be) to-God for seeing-you.
sentences.i: He said to me, “Know, my brother, that from the time I took to my bed I have not sat up until this hour. Praise be to God for the sight of you!”
sentences.n: min ḥīni raqadtu, “from the time I lay down”: ḥīn, “time”, stands in construct with a whole clause. mā jalastu illā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati, “I did not sit except at this hour”, I have only now sat up: mā with the perfect, the plain negative of past fact. ʿalā after al-ḥamdu li-Allāh marks what God is praised for. mushāhada, Form III verbal noun, “beholding”, the sight of you. The damma of رقدتُ and the shadda of الّا are printed.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَلَمْ أَزَلْ أُسْنِدُهُ حَتَّى أَوْقَفْتُهُ عَلَى رِجْلَيْهِ وَمَشَّيْتُهُ خُطُوَاتٍ وَغَيَّرْتُ أَثْوَابَهُ وَشَرِبَ شَرَابًا وَكُلُّ ذَلِكَ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَطِيبَ خَاطِرُهُ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-lam azal usniduhu ḥattā awqaftuhu ʿalā rijlayhi wa-mashshaytuhu khuṭuwātin wa-ghayyartu athwābahu wa-shariba sharāban wa-kullu dhālika li-ajli an yaṭība khāṭiruhu
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And I-did-not cease I-prop-him until I-stood-him on his-two-feet, and I-made-him-walk steps, and I-changed his-clothes, and he-drank a-drink; and all that (was) for-the-sake-of that his-mind be-good.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: I kept on supporting him until I had him standing on his feet, and walked him a few steps, and changed his clothes, and he took something to drink; and all this was to lift his spirits.
sentences.n: lam azal with an imperfect, “I did not cease (doing)”, I kept on. awqafa, Form IV of waqafa, “to make stand”: Classical prefers the plain waqafa used transitively, but awqafa is the common later form. mashshā, Form II of mashā, “to make walk”; its shadda and that of غيّرت are printed. khuṭuwātin, plural of khuṭwa, “a step”, accusative of extent. athwāb, plural of thawb, “garment”. sharāb, “a drink”: in this tale often wine, here perhaps no more than a cordial. ṭāba khāṭiruhu, “his mind became good”, he was cheered; yaṭība is subjunctive after an.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ عَلَيْهِ عَلَامَةَ الْعَافِيَةِ حَدَّثْتُهُ بِمَا كَانَ مِنَ الْجَارِيَةِ وَلَمْ يَسْمَعْنِي أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytu ʿalayhi ʿalāmata al-ʿāfiyati ḥaddathtuhu bi-mā kāna mina al-jāriyati wa-lam yasmaʿnī aḥadun
sentences.l: And when I-saw upon-him the sign of the well-being, I-told-him of what was from the slave-girl; and no-one heard-me.
sentences.i: When I saw the signs of returning health on him, I told him all that had passed with the slave-girl, with no one to overhear me.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha bi-, Form II, “to tell (someone) of”: bi- marks the matter told. mā kāna mina al-jāriyati, “what came from the slave-girl”, what she had said and done. wa-lam yasmaʿnī aḥadun, “and no one heard me”, a circumstantial clause: he took care to be overheard by no one.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُلْتُ لَهُ شُدَّ نَفْسَكَ وَحَيْلَكَ فَأَنَا أَعْرِفُ مَابِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qultu lahu shudda nafsaka wa-ḥaylaka fa-anā aʿrifu mā bika
sentences.l: Then I-said to-him: Tighten your-self and your-strength, for I know what (is) with-you.
sentences.i: Then I said to him, “Pull yourself together and gather your strength, for I know what ails you.”
sentences.n: shudda, imperative of shadda, “to tighten, make firm”; its shadda is printed. ḥayl, “strength, power”: shadda ḥaylahu, “to brace oneself”, is a phrase of later and spoken Arabic. mā bika, “what is with you”: bi- marks the one an affliction sits on. The print runs mā and bika together (مابك).

sentences.t: فَتَبَسَّمَ فَقُلْتُ لَهُ إِنَّكَ لَا تَجِدُ إِلَّا مَايَسُرُّكَ وَنُدَاوِيكَ
sentences.tr: fa-tabassama fa-qultu lahu innaka lā tajidu illā mā yasurruka wa-nudāwīka
sentences.l: And he-smiled; and I-said to-him: Indeed you do-not find except what gladdens-you, and we-will-treat-you.
sentences.i: He smiled, and I said to him, “You will find nothing but what will gladden you, and we shall make you well.”
sentences.n: lā tajidu illā, “you will not find except”, you will find only. sarra, “to gladden”; its shadda is printed, and the print runs mā and yasurruka together (مايسرّك). nudāwīka, “we shall treat you”, from dāwā, Form III, “to doctor”: the jeweller counts himself with the slave-girl and her mistress, whose news is the cure.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ أَمَرَ بِإِحْضَارِ الطَّعَامِ فَأَحْضَرُوهُ وَأَوْمَى إِلَى غِلْمَانِهِ فَتَفَرَّقُوا
sentences.tr: thumma inna ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin amara bi-iḥḍāri al-ṭaʿāmi fa-aḥḍarūhu wa-awmā ilā ghilmānihi fa-tafarraqū
sentences.l: Then (indeed) ʿAlī ibn Bakkār ordered (with) the bringing of the food, and they-brought-it; and he-signalled to his-lads, and they-dispersed.
sentences.i: Then ʿAlī ibn Bakkār ordered food to be brought, and they brought it; and he made a sign to his servants, and they withdrew.
sentences.n: After thumma inna, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār stands in the accusative as the noun of inna. amara bi-, “to give orders for”: the verb takes bi- for the thing commanded. iḥḍār, verbal noun of aḥḍara, Form IV, “to bring”. awmā, “he signalled”, is Classical awmaʾa (أومأ) with the final hamza softened to a long ā and spelt ى, a regular later form. tafarraqa, Form V, “to disperse”: he sent them off so that the two could talk alone. The shadda of فتفرّقوا is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِي يَا أَخِي هَلْ رَأَيْتَ مَا أَصَابَنِي
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lī yā akhī hal raʾayta mā aṣābanī
sentences.l: Then he-said to-me: O my-brother, have you-seen what befell-me?
sentences.i: Then he said to me, “My brother, have you seen what has befallen me?”
sentences.n: aṣāba, Form IV, “to strike, befall”. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: وَاعْتَذَرَلِي وَسَأَلَنِي عَنْ حَالِي فِي هَذِهِ الْمُدَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿtadhara lī wa-saʾalanī ʿan ḥālī fī hādhihi al-muddati
sentences.l: And he-excused-himself to-me, and he-asked-me about my-state in this period.
sentences.i: And he made his excuses to me, and asked me how I had fared all this while.
sentences.n: The print runs iʿtadhara and lī together (واعتذرلي); it is kept as one word. iʿtadhara li-, Form VIII, “to apologise to”: li- marks the one apologised to; he is sorry, it seems, for the trouble and loss his love has brought on the jeweller. mudda, “a space of time”. The hamza of سألني is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرْتُهُ بِجَمِيعِ مَاجَرَى لِي مِنَ الْأَوَّلِ إِلَى الْآخِرِ فَتَعَجَّبَ ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلْخَدَمِ ائْتُونِي بِكَذَا وَكَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhbartuhu bi-jamīʿi mā jarā lī mina al-awwali ilā al-ākhiri fa-taʿajjaba thumma qāla li-al-khadami iʾtūnī bi-kadhā wa-kadhā
sentences.l: And I-informed-him of all what happened to-me from the first to the last; and he-marvelled, then he-said to the servants: Bring-me such and such.
sentences.i: So I told him all that had happened to me, from first to last, and he was amazed. Then he said to the servants, “Bring me this and that.”
sentences.n: The jeweller is answering ʿAlī's question about how he had fared. akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks what is told. min al-awwali ilā al-ākhiri, “from the first to the last”; the madda of الآخر is the print's own. The print runs mā and jarā together (ماجرى). iʾtūnī, “bring me”, is the plural imperative of atā, “to come”, with bi- for the thing brought; its hamza is printed. bi-kadhā wa-kadhā, “with such and such”: the teller does not trouble to list the things.

sentences.t: فَأَتَوْهُ بِفَرْشٍ نَفِيسٍ وَبُسُطٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ تَعَالِيقِ الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ أَكْثَرَ مِنَ الَّذِي ضَاعَ لِي وَأَعْطَانِي إِيَّاهُ جَمِيعًا
sentences.tr: fa-atawhu bi-farshin nafīsin wa-busuṭin wa-ghayri dhālika min taʿālīqi al-dhahabi wa-al-fiḍḍati akthara mina alladhī ḍāʿa lī wa-aʿṭānī iyyāhu jamīʿan
sentences.l: And they-brought-him precious furnishing and carpets and other-than that, of hangings of the gold and the silver, more than that-which was-lost to-me; and he-gave-me it all-together.
sentences.i: They brought him costly furnishings and carpets, and other things besides, hangings of gold and silver, more than I had lost; and he gave me the whole of it.
sentences.n: atā bi-, “to come with”, to bring. farsh, “furnishing”, the rugs, mattresses and cushions of a room; busuṭ, plural of bisāṭ, “carpet”. taʿālīq, plural of taʿlīq, “things hung up”: lamps, chains and ornaments. akthara, “more”, in the accusative, describing the whole gift; in ḍāʿa lī, “was lost to me”, li- marks the loser. aʿṭānī iyyāhu, “he gave me it”: when a verb has two pronoun objects, the second is carried by iyyā-. ʿAlī is making good the goods stolen from the jeweller's house by the thieves.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلْتُهُ إِلَى مَنْزِلِي وَأَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهُ لَيْلَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-arsaltuhu ilā manzilī wa-aqamtu ʿindahu laylatī
sentences.l: And I-sent-it to my-house, and I-stayed with-him my-night.
sentences.i: I sent it all to my house, and stayed the night with him.
sentences.n: arsaltuhu, “I sent it”: the -hu is the gift as one whole. laylatī, “my night”, accusative of time: that night.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَسْفَرَ الصُّبْحُ قَٰلَ لِي اعْلَمْ أَنَّ لِكُلِّ شَئٍ نِهَايَةً وَنِهَايَةُ الْهَوَى الْمَوْتُ أَوِ الْوِصَالُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā asfara al-ṣubḥu qāla lī iʿlam anna li-kulli shayʾin nihāyatan wa-nihāyatu al-hawā al-mawtu awi al-wiṣālu
sentences.l: And when the morning shone-forth, he-said to-me: Know that to every thing (is) an-end, and the end of the passion (is) the death or the union.
sentences.i: When the morning broke he said to me, “Know that everything has its end, and the end of love is death or union.
sentences.n: asfara, Form IV, “to shine forth”, of the dawn uncovering the sky. The print spells qāla as قل, pointed here with a dagger alif. li-kulli shayʾin nihāyatan, “to every thing an end”: li- of possession, and nihāyatan is the noun of anna, so accusative. The print spells shayʾ as شئ, the hamza on a yāʾ-seat with no separate yāʾ; the hamza is its own. wiṣāl, “union”, the lovers' coming together, set against death as the only two ways love can end.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا إِلَى الْمَوْتِ أَقْرَبُ فَيَا لَيْتَنِي مِتُّ قَبْلَ الَّذِي جَرَى
sentences.tr: wa-anā ilā al-mawti aqrabu fa-yā laytanī mittu qabla alladhī jarā
sentences.l: And I (am) to the death nearer; so O would-that-I had-died before that-which happened.
sentences.i: And I am the nearer to death. Oh, would that I had died before what has happened!
sentences.n: ilā al-mawti aqrabu, “nearer to death”: the elative takes ilā for what one is near to. yā laytanī, “O would that I”: yā only gives the wish its cry. mittu, “I died”, is the form of māta with i that is usual in the first person (beside muttu); the shadda is the print's own. alladhī jarā, “what happened”, the night of the thieves and the watch.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا أَنَّ اللَّهَ لَطَفَ بِنَا لَافْتَضَحْنَا وَلَا أَدْرِي مَا الَّذِي يُوصِلُنِي إِلَى الْخَلَاصِ مِمَّا أَنَا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā anna Allāha laṭafa binā la-iftaḍaḥnā wa-lā adrī mā alladhī yūṣilunī ilā al-khalāṣi mimmā anā fīhi
sentences.l: And were-it-not that God was-gracious to-us, we-would-have-been-disgraced; and I-do-not know what (is) that-which will-bring-me to the deliverance from-what I (am) in-it.
sentences.i: Had God not been gracious to us, we should have been put to shame; and I do not know what can bring me deliverance from the state I am in.
sentences.n: lawlā anna …, “were it not that …”, is answered by la- with the perfect: la-iftaḍaḥnā, “we would have been disgraced”. iftaḍaḥa, Form VIII of faḍaḥa, “to be exposed, shamed”: had the watch not let them go, the lovers' secret would have been out. laṭafa bi-, “to be gracious to”: bi- marks the one shown kindness. mā alladhī, “what is it that”; awṣala ilā, Form IV, “to bring to”. mimmā anā fīhi, “from what I am in”, my present plight.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا خَوْفِي مِنَ اللَّهِ لَعَجَّلْتُ عَلَى نَفْسِى بِالْهَلَاكِ
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā khawfī mina Allāhi la-ʿajjaltu ʿalā nafsī bi-al-halāki
sentences.l: And were-it-not-for my-fear of God, I-would-have-hastened upon my-self the destruction.
sentences.i: And were it not for my fear of God, I would have hastened my own end.
sentences.n: He means he would have taken his own life; what holds him back is fear of God, since self-murder is a sin. lawlā with a plain noun, “but for”. ʿajjala ʿalā nafsihi bi-al-halāki, “to hasten destruction upon oneself”: ʿalā marks the one it falls on, bi- the thing hastened. نفسى is printed with final ى; the shadda of لعجّلت is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ يَا أَخِي أَنَّنِي كَالطَّيْرِ فِى الْقَفَصِ وَأَنَّ نَفْسِي هَالِكَةٌ لَا مَحَالَةَ مِنَ الْغُصَصِ وَلَكِنْ لَهَا وَقْتٌ مَعْلُومٌ وَأَجَلٌ مَحْتُومٌ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam yā akhī annanī ka-al-ṭayri fī al-qafaṣi wa-anna nafsī hālikatun lā maḥālata mina al-ghuṣaṣi wa-lākin lahā waqtun maʿlūmun wa-ajalun maḥtūmun
sentences.l: And know, O my-brother, that-I (am) like-the-bird in the cage, and that my-soul (is) perishing, no escape, from the chokings; but for-it (is) a-time known and a-term decreed.
sentences.i: Know, my brother, that I am like a bird in a cage, and that my soul must surely perish of the griefs that choke me; but it has its known time and its appointed term.”
sentences.n: The speech falls into rhymed prose: qafaṣ / ghuṣaṣ, then maʿlūm / maḥtūm. ṭayr is properly a collective, “birds”, here used of one bird. ghuṣaṣ, plural of ghuṣṣa, “a choking”, a lump in the throat, and so a grief that stops the breath; min gives the cause, perishing “of” griefs. lā maḥālata, “there is no escape”, inevitably. lahā, “it has”: li- of possession. ajal, “term”, the appointed hour of death; maḥtūm, “decreed, sealed”. فى is printed with final ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى وَاشْتَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā wa-ishtakā wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: Then he-wept and complained, and he-recited, saying — verse:
sentences.i: Then he wept and lamented, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: bakā / ishtakā, “he wept / he complained”, a small rhymed pair. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”. شعر, “verse”, is the print's rubric announcing the poem.

sentences.t:
لَقَدْ كَفَى مَاجَرَى لِلصَّبِّ مَدْمَعُهُ * اَمَّا الْاَسَى عَنْ جَمِيعِ الصَّبْرِ يَرْدَعُهُ
قَدْ كَانَ يَجْمَعُ لِلْاَسْرَارِ كَاتِمُهَا * فَفَرَّقَتْ عَيْنُهُ مَا كَانَ يَجْمَعُهُ
sentences.tr:
laqad kafā mā jarā li-al-ṣabbi madmaʿuhu * ammā al-asā ʿan jamīʿi al-ṣabri yardaʿuhu
qad kāna yajmaʿu li-al-asrāri kātimuhā * fa-farraqat ʿaynuhu mā kāna yajmaʿuhu
sentences.l:
Indeed it-has-sufficed, what has-run for the ardent-lover, his-tear-flow; * as-for the grief, from all the patience it-holds-him-back.
It-had-been gathering (to) the secrets, their-keeper, * then his-eye scattered what he-had-been gathering-it.
sentences.i:
The lover has shed tears enough; and grief still holds him back from any patience.
The keeper of secrets long hoarded them, till his own eye scattered all that he had hoarded.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ, rhyming in -ʿuhu. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَمَّا, الْاَسَى and لِلْاَسْرَارِ, where the edition marks no hamza. ṣabb, “one burning with love”; madmaʿ, the place tears flow from, and so the flow itself: mā jarā … madmaʿuhu, “what his tears have run”, is the subject of kafā, “has sufficed”. ammā, “as for”, normally has its answer opened by fa- (fa-yardaʿuhu); the line leaves it out, as verse sometimes does. radaʿa ʿan, “to hold back from”. In the second line li-al-asrāri marks the object of yajmaʿu, and kātimuhā, “their keeper”, is its subject: the lover who long kept his secret is betrayed by his tears, since the eye, ʿayn, feminine, “scattered” what he had gathered.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ لَهُ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ يَاسَيِّدِي اعْلَمْ أَنِّي عَوَّلْتُ عَلَى الذَّهَابِ إِلَى دَارِي فَلَعَلَّ الْجَارِيَةَ تَرْجِعُ إِلَيَّ بِخَبَرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla lahu al-jawhariyyu yā sayyidī iʿlam annī ʿawwaltu ʿalā al-dhahābi ilā dārī fa-laʿalla al-jāriyata tarjiʿu ilayya bi-khabarin
sentences.l: And when he-finished from his-verse, the jeweller said to-him: O my-master, know that-I have-resolved upon the going to my-house; for perhaps the slave-girl will-return to-me with news.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses, the jeweller said to him, “Sir, I have made up my mind to go home; perhaps the slave-girl will come back to me with news.”
sentences.n: For a moment the telling slips out of the jeweller's mouth: he is “the jeweller” who “said to him”, as Shahrazād would put it, and in the next sentence but one he is “I” again. ʿawwala ʿalā, Form II, “to rely on”, and so “to resolve on”. laʿalla, “perhaps”, puts its noun in the accusative (al-jāriyata). rajaʿa bi-, “to come back with”. The print runs yā and sayyidī together (ياسيدي); the shadda of اليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ لَا بَأْسَ بِذَلِكَ وَلَكِنِ اذْهَبْ وَأَسْرِعْ بِالْعَوْدِ عِنْدِي لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تُخْبِرَنِي فَإِنَّكَ تَرَى حَالِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin lā baʾsa bi-dhālika wa-lākini idhhab wa-asriʿ bi-al-ʿawdi ʿindī li-ajli an tukhbiranī fa-innaka tarā ḥālī
sentences.l: And ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said: No harm in that; but go, and hasten with the return at-me, for-the-sake-of that you-tell-me, for you see my-state.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said, “There is no harm in that. But go, and make haste to come back to me and tell me; for you see how it is with me.”
sentences.n: lā baʾsa bi-, “there is no harm in”; the print writes baʾs without its hamza (باس). asraʿa bi-, “to hurry with”, make haste over; ʿawd, “return”, the verbal noun of ʿāda. ʿindī, “at me”, stands where Classical Arabic would say ilayya, “to me”: a Middle Arabic use after a verb of motion. li-ajli an, “for the sake of that”, so that, with the subjunctive tukhbiranī.

sentences.t: فَوَدَّعْتُهُ وَانْصَرَفْتُ إِلَى دَارِي فَلَمْ أَسْتَتِمَّ الْجُلُوسَ إِلَّا وَالْجَارِيَةُ أَقْبَلَتْ وَهِيَ مُخْتَنِقَةٌ بِالْبُكَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-waddaʿtuhu wa-inṣaraftu ilā dārī fa-lam astatimma al-julūsa illā wa-al-jāriyatu aqbalat wa-hiya mukhtaniqatun bi-al-bukāʾi
sentences.l: And I-bade-him-farewell and I-went-away to my-house; and I-had-not completed the sitting except (that) the slave-girl came-forward, she choking with the weeping.
sentences.i: So I took my leave of him and went home; and I had scarcely sat down when the slave-girl came in, choking with tears.
sentences.n: lam … illā wa-, “I had not … but that”, no sooner … than: the wa- opens a clause for what happens at that very moment. astatimma, jussive of istatamma, Form X, “to complete”: the doubled letter stays together and takes a fatḥa. mukhtaniqa, Form VIII participle of khanaqa, “choking”; bi- names what she chokes on. The shadda of فودّعتُه and the damma on its tāʾ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَا سَبَبُ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā mā sababu dhālika
sentences.l: And I-said to-her: What (is) the cause of that?
sentences.i: I said to her, “What is the reason for this?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَاسَيِّدِي اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ حَلَّ بِنَا مَا حَلَّ مِنْ أَمْرٍ نَخَافُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yā sayyidī iʿlam annahu ḥalla binā mā ḥalla min amrin nakhāfuhu
sentences.l: And she-said: O my-master, know that-it (is that) there-befell us what befell, of a-matter we-fear-it.
sentences.i: She said, “Sir, know that there has befallen us what has befallen: the very thing we feared.
sentences.n: annahu, “that it (is the case that)”: -hu is the pronoun of the matter, pointing to the clause that follows. ḥalla bi-, “to befall”: bi- marks those it lights on. mā ḥalla, “what befell”, is left vague, and min amrin nakhāfuhu, “of a matter we fear”, says what kind of thing it was. The shaddas of both حلّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي لَمَّا مَضَيْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِكَ بِالْأَمْسِ صَادَفْتُ سَيِّدَتِي وَهِيَ مُغْتَاظَةٌ عَلَى وَصِيفَةٍ مِنَ الْوَصِيفَتَيْنِ اللَّتَيْنِ كَانَتَا مَعَنَا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ فَأَمَرَتْ بِضَرْبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-innī lammā maḍaytu min ʿindika bi-al-amsi ṣādaftu sayyidatī wa-hiya mughtāẓatun ʿalā waṣīfatin mina al-waṣīfatayni allatayni kānatā maʿanā tilka al-laylata fa-amarat bi-ḍarbihā
sentences.l: For I, when I-went from with-you yesterday, I-came-upon my-lady, and she (was) enraged at a-maid of the two-maids who were with-us that night; and she-ordered her-beating.
sentences.i: When I left you yesterday, I found my mistress in a rage with one of the two maids who had been with us that night, and she ordered her to be beaten.
sentences.n: bi-al-amsi, “yesterday”. ṣādafa, Form III, “to come upon, find”. mughtāẓa, Form VIII participle of ghāẓa, “filled with rage”; ʿalā marks the one she is angry with. The two maids (waṣīfa) are the ones who were with Shams al-Nahār at the jeweller's house on the night of the thieves; allatayni and kānatā are feminine dual. amara bi-, “to order”: the verb chooses bi-, which marks the thing ordered, here ḍarbihā, “her beating”.

sentences.t: فَخَافَتْ وَهَرَبَتْ مِنْ سَيِّدَتِهَا فَخَرَجَتْ فَلَاقَاهَا بَعْضُ الْمُوَكَّلِينَ بِالْبَابِ فَأَخَذَهَا وَأَرَادَ رَدَّهَا إِلَى سَيِّدَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-khāfat wa-harabat min sayyidatihā fa-kharajat fa-lāqāhā baʿḍu al-muwakkalīna bi-al-bābi fa-akhadhahā wa-arāda raddahā ilā sayyidatihā
sentences.l: And she-was-afraid and fled from her-mistress, and she-went-out; and one of the (ones) set-over the gate met-her, and he-took-her and wanted her-returning to her-mistress.
sentences.i: The maid took fright and ran away from her mistress and got out of the house; and one of the men set to guard the gate met her, seized her, and meant to take her back to her mistress.
sentences.n: baʿḍu al-muwakkalīna, “some of those set over”, here simply “one of them”, since the verbs after it are singular. muwakkal bi-, “appointed to”, a guard posted at the gate. lāqā, Form III, “to meet”. arāda raddahā, “he wanted her sending-back”: radd, the verbal noun of radda, with the maid as its object suffix.

sentences.t: فَلَوَّحَتْ لَهُ بِالْكَلَامِ فَلَاطَفَهَا وَاسْتَنْطَقَهَا عَنْ حَالِهَا فَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِمَا كُنَّا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lawwaḥat lahu bi-al-kalāmi fa-lāṭafahā wa-istanṭaqahā ʿan ḥālihā fa-akhbarathu bi-mā kunnā fīhi
sentences.l: And she-hinted to-him with the speech, and he-treated-her-gently and made-her-speak about her-state, and she-told-him of-what we-were in-it.
sentences.i: She let fall some hints to him; and he coaxed her and drew her out about her situation, and she told him all that we had been about.
sentences.n: lawwaḥa, Form II, “to make a sign, hint”; li- marks the one hinted to, bi-al-kalāmi, “in speech”, the means: she let something slip. lāṭafa, Form III, “to treat kindly, coax”. istanṭaqa, Form X of naṭaqa, “to make speak”, to question. akhbara bi-, “to inform of”; mā kunnā fīhi, “what we were in”, the lovers' secret meetings. The shaddas of فلوّحت and كنّا are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَبَلَغَ الْخَبَرُ إِلَى الْخَلِيفَةِ فَأَمَرَ بِنَقْلِ سَيِّدَتِي شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَجَمِيعِ مَالِهَا إِلَى دَارِ الْخِلَافَةِ وَوَكَّلَ بِهَا عِشْرِينَ خَادِمًا
sentences.tr: fa-balagha al-khabaru ilā al-khalīfati fa-amara bi-naqli sayyidatī Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-jamīʿi mālihā ilā dāri al-khilāfati wa-wakkala bihā ʿishrīna khādiman
sentences.l: And the news reached to the Caliph, and he-ordered the moving of my-lady Shams al-Nahār and all her-wealth to the house of the Caliphate, and he-set over-her twenty servants.
sentences.i: The news reached the Caliph, and he ordered my lady Shams al-Nahār and all she owned to be moved to the palace of the Caliphate, and set twenty eunuchs to watch over her.
sentences.n: balagha ilā, “to reach”: Classical balagha takes its object directly. amara bi-naqli, “he ordered the moving of”. مالها is read mālihā, “her wealth”; it could also be mā lahā, “what was hers”, with the same sense. dār al-khilāfa, the Caliph's own palace, where she will be under his eye. wakkala bi-, Form II, “to set (someone) over”: bi- marks the one guarded. khādim, “servant”, in a palace usually a eunuch; after ʿishrīn the counted noun stands in the accusative singular. The shadda of ووكّل is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَجْتَمِعْ بِهَا إِلَى الْآنَ وَلَمْ أُعْلِمْهَا بِالسَّبَبِ وَتَوَهَّمْتُ أَنَّهُ بِسَبَبِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam ajtamiʿ bihā ilā al-āna wa-lam uʿlimhā bi-al-sababi wa-tawahhamtu annahu bi-sababi dhālika
sentences.l: And I-have-not met with-her until now, and I-have-not informed-her of the cause; and I-supposed that-it (was) by-reason-of that.
sentences.i: I have not been able to see her to this moment, nor to tell her the reason; but I suppose it was because of that.
sentences.n: ijtamaʿa bi-, “to meet with”. ولم اعلمها is read lam uʿlimhā bi-al-sababi, “I have not informed her of the cause”, Form IV aʿlama with bi- for what is told: the girl has had no chance to tell her mistress how the secret got out. The letters also allow lam aʿlamhā, “I have not learnt it”, a loose way of saying she does not know the cause for certain, which would sit well with tawahhamtu, “I supposed”. tawahhama, Form V, “to imagine, suspect”. The madda of الآن is printed.

sentences.t: فَخَشِيتُ أَنَا عَلَى نَفْسِي وَاحْتَرْتُ يَاسَيِّدِي وَلَمْ أَدْرِ كَيْفَ أَفْعَلُ وَكَيْفَ أَحْتَالُ فِي أَمْرِي وَأَمْرِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-khashītu anā ʿalā nafsī wa-iḥtartu yā sayyidī wa-lam adri kayfa afʿalu wa-kayfa aḥtālu fī amrī wa-amrihimā
sentences.l: And I-feared, I, for my-self, and I-became-perplexed, O my-master, and I-did-not know how I-act and how I-contrive in my-affair and the-affair-of-the-two-of-them.
sentences.i: So I have come to fear for myself, sir, and I am at my wits' end: I do not know what to do, or how to find a way through, for myself or for the two of them.
sentences.n: khashiya ʿalā, “to fear for”; anā underlines the “I”. iḥtāra, Form VIII of ḥāra, “to be at a loss”; the damma on its tāʾ is printed. lam adri, jussive of darā, with the final vowel cut short. iḥtāla, Form VIII, “to use a ruse, contrive”. amrihimā, “the affair of the two of them”, Shams al-Nahār and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ مَا عِنْدَهَا أَحْفَظُ وَأَقْرَبُ لِكِتْمَانِ السِّرِّ غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-inna mā ʿindahā aḥfaẓu wa-aqrabu li-kitmāni al-sirri ghayrī
sentences.l: For (indeed) not with-her (is one) better-keeping and nearer to the hiding of the secret, other-than-me.
sentences.i: For she has no one about her, besides me, more trustworthy or better fitted to keep the secret.
sentences.n: The sentence is loosely built. It is read with mā as “not”: “there is not with her (anyone) better at keeping and fitter for hiding the secret, other than me”, that is, she has no one but the girl to trust, so the task falls to her. inna then stands before a whole clause with no noun of its own, as if “for the case is that …”. aḥfaẓu and aqrabu are elatives, “better at keeping”, “nearer, fitter”; li- names what one is fit for. Taking mā as “what” gives no clear sense. The girl's speech breaks off here with the night and goes on in the next.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning that overtakes. Here the print sets the name as one word (شهرزاد). al-kalām al-mubāḥ, “the permitted speech”; the rhyme ṣabāḥ / mubāḥ closes every night.
